item.title: About This Resource & How We Research
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
This resource helps people find the official legal status of keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting a domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) wherever they live, and what to do about it.

Legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

What this is, and is not

It is a research aid built from official government sources. It is not legal advice, and we are not lawyers. Laws change, and local officials interpret them in ways we cannot control. Always read the official source yourself and, when it matters, confirm directly with the agency before you act.

How we research each jurisdiction

  • We start from official primary sources: statutes, regulations, and the responsible agencies (wildlife, agriculture, customs).
  • We use structured deep research, then verify every claim against the official source and link it.
  • Where the published rules are unclear, we say so, and where possible we confirm directly with the agency in writing.
  • Every answer carries a confidence level and a last-verified date. Pages we have not yet agency-confirmed are marked preliminary.

What the labels mean

LegalAllowed, with no special permit.
Legal with a permitAllowed, but a permit, license, or registration is required.
RestrictedAllowed only under specific conditions or limits.
ProhibitedNot allowed.
Unregulated / unclearNo rule found, or the law is silent or ambiguous.
Not yet researchedNot yet researched. Here is how you can help.

Species, not domestication

An important nuance: most laws regulate a species, not whether your animals are tame. A domesticated roof rat is still Rattus rattus. So an exemption for “domestic” animals (which often means only Rattus norvegicus (the fancy rat)) may or may not cover a roof rat. We flag this wherever it matters, and it is often the heart of the advocacy case for fairer rules.

Help us keep it accurate

Found something out of date, or know the rule for your area? Please tell us, ideally with a link to the official source, and we will verify and update. This resource gets better with every contribution.

item.title: How to Find Your Local Law (Step by Step)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Can’t find your area in our guide yet? Here is exactly how to get the official answer for where you live, the same way we do it. It usually takes a few emails.

Legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Step 1: Know the exact animal

The pet roof rat is Rattus rattus. When you contact an agency, use the scientific name and make clear the animals are captive-bred and kept as pets, not wild-caught. (also relevant: it is a different species from Rattus norvegicus, the fancy rat). Many rules that exempt “domestic” animals mean only that other species, so do not assume.

Step 2: Identify your jurisdiction(s)

Rules can stack at three levels: your country, your state or region, and your city or county. Check all three; a permissive country can still have a local ban, and vice versa.

Instant tool: check your city or county ordinance

The local layer is the hardest to research, because most city and county animal ordinances live in databases that are not indexed well by ordinary search. This finder builds targeted searches of the major municipal-code libraries for your area, scoped to the words that matter.

Instant city / county ordinance finder

Local rules are the hardest layer to find. Type your city or region, and this builds ready-made searches of the major municipal-code libraries (Municode, American Legal Publishing, eCode360) plus a plain web search, for the words that matter. It opens an ordinary web search in a new tab; nothing is sent to us.

Once you are in your code, search these terms: rodent, exotic animal, wild animal, prohibited animal, number of pets / pet limit. Found your rule? Tell us and we will add your city.

Step 3: Ask the right agencies

  • Wildlife agency: non-native and captive-wildlife rules, a common place a non-traditional pet is regulated.
  • Agriculture / animal-health department: sale, dealer licensing, and import health certificates.
  • Customs / border or import authority: bringing animals across borders.
  • Local animal control or city clerk: city and county ordinances.

Step 4: Ask the questions, in writing

Email each agency and ask, specifically, about a roof rat kept as a pet:

  • Is it legal to keep one as a pet? Any permit or registration?
  • Is it legal to breed them? Any license?
  • Is it legal to sell or give them to others? Any dealer license?
  • What is required to transport or import them (health certificate, permit)?

Ask for the answer in writing and for the specific statute or rule, so you have a record and a citation. Write to the agency in the official language of your country.

Step 5: Get it in writing, and share it

Save the agency’s reply. Then please send it to us with the source links so we can verify it and add your area to the guide, helping the next person who asks.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Arab Emirates

Summary. The UAE is now AGENCY-CONFIRMED PROHIBITED for private roof rats, and it is a textbook species-not-domestication case. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that the 'domesticated rats' exemption to the rodent-keeping restriction under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). Because the roof rat (R. rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, private individuals may not keep, breed, possess, or import it; the only import pathway is for licensed research entities or zoological facilities. (An earlier reading that the exemption might cover domesticated R. rattus is closed by MOCCAE's species-specific reply.)

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE), written reply June 2026: the 'domesticated rats' exemption to the rodent-keeping restriction under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). The roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, so private individuals may not keep, breed, possess, or import it; importation is restricted to licensed research entities or zoological facilities.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

MOCCAE confirmed in writing (June 2026) that the 'domesticated rats' exemption under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus); the roof rat (R. rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, so private individuals may not keep it. A textbook species-not-domestication prohibition.

Sources: UAE Federal Legislation Portal, Official UAE Government Portal

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Prohibited for private individuals: MOCCAE (June 2026) confirmed R. rattus may not be kept, bred, or possessed privately; only the fancy rat is within the exemption.

Sources: MOCCAE, UAE Federal Legislation Portal

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Prohibited for private individuals: since R. rattus may not be privately kept/bred/possessed (MOCCAE, June 2026), private sale or transfer is not permitted either.

Sources: UAE Federal Legislation Portal, MOCCAE

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Import is prohibited for private individuals (MOCCAE, June 2026): there is no private-owner import permit pathway for R. rattus; importation is restricted strictly to licensed research entities or zoological facilities. Never release.

Sources: MOCCAE, MOCCAE (mirrored)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a domesticated roof rat is exempt from the UAE dangerous-animal ban (no keeper permit). Commercial breeding/selling needs a MOCCAE animal-care-activities licence + a local commercial licence; importing needs a MOCCAE live-animal import permit (AED 100) + the rodent veterinary health certificate. ⚠️ Confirm with MOCCAE that 'domesticated rats' in the Annex covers captive-bred R. rattus. Never release.
  • For import: apply for the MOCCAE live-animal import permit + obtain the rodent health certificate from the origin country
  • For commercial breeding/sale: MOCCAE animal-care-activities licence + local DED/municipal licence
  • Confirm R. rattus species-scope with MOCCAE

Forms: MOCCAE — Import Permit for Live Animals and Birds · Where: Ministry of Climate Change & Environment (MOCCAE) · Fees: Import permit AED 100

Source: MOCCAE, MOCCAE

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in United Arab Emirates. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in United Arab Emirates

The UAE bars private individuals from keeping most rodents but exempts 'domesticated rats'. MOCCAE has confirmed it reads that exemption to mean ONLY the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) — so a captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (R. rattus) is prohibited to keep, breed, or import, even though it is just as domesticated. This is a classification gap, not a safety judgment.

The ask: Ask MOCCAE to recognize captive-bred, multi-generation domesticated Rattus rattus as a 'domesticated rat' within the existing Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 exemption (the same exemption the fancy rat enjoys), or to set out a private-keeper pathway. The animals are tame, indoor-kept, and never released.

Where the lever really is: MOCCAE confirmed this is its classification under the regulation, so the lever is the agency/regulator: ask MOCCAE to read the 'domesticated rats' exemption to include domesticated R. rattus (an interpretation/classification change). If MOCCAE says only a regulatory amendment can do it, that points to the rule-making authority. It is not a courts matter.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) (executive / agency) — info@moccae.gov.ae
    MOCCAE administers Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 and decides which rats count as 'domesticated'; it replies to written inquiries (verified, June 2026).

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment,

Under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016, individuals may keep 'domesticated rats', but I understand the Ministry currently reads this to cover only the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), excluding the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus).

I respectfully ask the Ministry to recognize captive-bred, multi-generation domesticated Rattus rattus as a 'domesticated rat' within this exemption, the same way the fancy rat is treated. These animals are selectively bred for tameness over many generations, kept indoors as companion animals, and never released; they pose no greater risk than the fancy rat already permitted.

If recognition requires a regulatory step, I would be grateful to know the process. Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
العربية
إلى وزارة التغير المناخي والبيئة الموقرة،

بموجب القانون الاتحادي رقم 22 لسنة 2016، يُسمح للأفراد بتربية «الجرذان المستأنسة»، إلا أنني أتفهم أن الوزارة تفسّر ذلك حالياً على أنه يشمل فقط الجرذ النرويجي (Rattus norvegicus)، مع استثناء الجرذ الأسود المستأنس (Rattus rattus).

أرجو من الوزارة الكريمة الاعتراف بالجرذ الأسود (Rattus rattus) المربّى في الأسر عبر أجيال متعددة باعتباره «جرذاً مستأنساً» ضمن هذا الاستثناء، تماماً كما يُعامَل الجرذ النرويجي. فهذه الحيوانات تُنتخب للأُلفة عبر أجيال عديدة، وتُربّى داخل المنازل كحيوانات أليفة، ولا تُطلق في البيئة أبداً، وهي لا تشكّل خطراً أكبر من الجرذ النرويجي المسموح به بالفعل.

وإذا كان هذا الاعتراف يتطلب إجراءً تنظيمياً، فسأكون ممتناً لمعرفة الآلية. شكراً لكم على حسن اهتمامكم.

[الاسم]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 (dangerous animals) + Annex 1 — Rodents: 'All species except domesticated hamsters, guinea pigs, rats and mice' — UAE Federal Legislation Portal
  • u.ae — Banning private ownership of dangerous animals (official summary) — Official UAE Government Portal
  • MOCCAE — Import Permit for Live Animals and Birds (AED 100, 90-day; rodents covered) — MOCCAE
  • MOCCAE — Veterinary Health Certificate model for exporting rodents/lagomorphs/reptiles to the UAE — MOCCAE (mirrored)
  • MOCCAE — License for Practicing Animal Care Activities (breeding/import-export) — MOCCAE

Search terms: Rattus rattus, الجرذ الأسود, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Argentina? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Argentina

Summary. Argentina classifies the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1, 'especie restringida y de control obligatorio') under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution imposes a blanket federal ban on the breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release, importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species — so breeding, selling/giving, and transport of a roof rat are prohibited, with no lawful permit pathway (the Art. 5 ban preempts the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry of Res. 170/2021). Private possession ('tenencia') of a pre-existing captive-bred specimen sits in a deliberate gap: Art. 5 enumerates banned actions but omits passive possession, and the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19) means no one can be deprived of what the law does not forbid — so keeping is best read as unregulated/unclear rather than expressly legal, and a province or municipality could still add a local ban. The brown/fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is taxonomically EEI-1 too, yet is sold and kept openly thanks to a de-facto domestication exemption — an exemption R. rattus, lacking any recognized domestic lineage, does not enjoy.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar), written reply 2026-06-11: 'Esta Dirección de Biodiversidad interviene solamente animales silvestres. Por la tenencia de un animal doméstico, consulte ante la autoridad jurisdiccional correspondiente al lugar donde se encuentre el ejemplar.' (This Biodiversity Directorate only intervenes for WILD animals; for the possession of a DOMESTIC animal, consult the provincial/jurisdictional authority where the specimen is located.) — the federal wildlife authority disclaims jurisdiction over the keeping (tenencia) of a domestic specimen, confirming that possession of a kept R. rattus is a provincial matter rather than a federal wild-fauna question.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 enumerates the banned activities for EEI-1 species — cría, compra/venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional, and movimiento interjurisdiccional — but conspicuously omits 'tenencia' (passive private possession). Under the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19: no inhabitant may be deprived of what the law does not forbid), merely keeping a pre-existing captive-bred R. rattus indoors is not an enumerated federal offense, so federal authorities have no Art. 5 mandate to confiscate it. This is a jurisprudential gap, not an affirmative protected right: provinces and municipalities retain the police power to enact stricter local bans on keeping invasive rodents, and federal silence does not equal permission. Treat as unregulated/unclear — neither expressly authorized nor expressly prohibited.

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg), Constitución de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg), Sistema de Información de Biodiversidad / APN

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'su cría o cultivo' for EEI-1 species in places under national jurisdiction, with no hobbyist or small-breeder threshold. Because R. rattus is EEI-1, the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad is legally stripped of authority to grant any breeding license, and the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021) — so even a fully compliant criadero application would be administratively dead on arrival. There is no lawful private or commercial pathway to breed the species; any breeding is treated as an illicit act of wildlife trafficking. (By contrast, R. norvegicus is bred openly under a de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not share.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'compra y venta, donación' of EEI-1 species — covering both sale and non-commercial gifting/donation. There is no lawful avenue to commercialize or transfer R. rattus: the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021), so no dealer/criadero license can issue, and even gifting is enumerated as a banned act. This forecloses any private give-away as well as commercial sale. (R. norvegicus is sold openly only because of an uncodified de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not formally enjoy.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 imposes a blanket ban on 'la introducción al territorio nacional y el movimiento interjurisdiccional' of EEI-1 species, so both importing R. rattus and moving it across provincial lines are prohibited. On import, the SENASA sanitary pathway (CVI, TAD, SIGTrámites) is entirely subordinate to the environmental veto: the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad must authorize a wildlife import first (Decreto 666/1997 Art. 22 empowers it to reject ecologically harmful imports), and for an EEI-1 species it is obligated to refuse — so SENASA can never issue the final entry permit. Internally, provincial fauna authorities cannot issue a transit guide (guía de tránsito) for a federally restricted EEI-1 species for personal relocation, leaving the animal legally trapped in its current province. No lawful transport pathway exists. (Intra-provincial movement within a single jurisdiction is not reached by the inter-jurisdictional ban, but the keep status governs there.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Poder Ejecutivo Nacional (Argentina.gob.ar), SENASA (Servicio Nacional de Sanidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1), Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 bans breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release (liberación), importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement, with no lawful permit pathway — the EEI-1 status strips the wildlife directorate of authority to license the species and preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021). Passive private possession ('tenencia') is not on the Art. 5 ban list, but a possessor is then locked in: cannot lawfully breed it, give it away, sell its offspring, or move it across provinces. Provinces/municipalities may add stricter local bans. Never release — liberation is expressly prohibited.
  • Do NOT breed, sell, give away, import, or move R. rattus across provincial lines — these are banned for EEI-1 species (Res. 109/2021 Art. 5)
  • Never release a roof rat into the environment (liberación is expressly prohibited)
  • If advocating: ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad for a written clarification on tenencia and a possible Art. 6 exception extending R. norvegicus-style domestic treatment to captive-bred R. rattus

Where: Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente) for clarifications/exceptions; SENASA for import questions; provincial fauna authority for transit

Source: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Poder Ejecutivo Nacional (Argentina.gob.ar)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Argentina

In Argentina the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution bans the breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species, and because the species is EEI-1 the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad has no authority to issue a breeder/operator license for it — so the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021) is foreclosed. The striking part is that the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) carries the IDENTICAL EEI-1 listing, yet it is bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because authorities treat its century-old laboratory/fancy strains as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. R. rattus simply never received that institutional recognition, so a tame, captive-bred roof rat is hit with the full force of the invasive-wildlife prohibitions purely on the basis of its species name. Separately, private possession ('tenencia') is conspicuously absent from the Art. 5 ban list, leaving a captive owner in a gray zone — not prosecuted for merely keeping the animal, but unable to lawfully breed, give, sell, or move it.

The ask: Ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad to confirm in writing (a) that passive private possession of a pre-existing captive-bred Rattus rattus, kept indoors and never released, is not among the activities banned by Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021; and (b) whether a formal regulatory exception exists or can be granted — via Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence — that extends to captive-bred, closed-colony R. rattus the same de-facto 'domestic animal' treatment already afforded to R. norvegicus, so that documented captive-bred specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization/transport prohibitions. The argument is the directorate's own line between wild and domestic: domestication, not wild ancestry, is what makes an animal a domestic companion — the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic, and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) earned the same recognition despite a wild origin. A multi-generation captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated on identical terms, so the question is simply whether the agency will extend the domestic recognition it already applies to its near-twin. For anyone importing, ask SENASA whether an EEI-1-classified companion rodent is automatically rejected in the TAD system, or whether a Certificado Veterinario Internacional can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen with a biosecurity plan.

Where the lever really is: Lever = the AGENCY (Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad), NOT the legislature. No statute names or bans R. rattus by species; the prohibition flows entirely from an administrative classification (EEI-1 under Resolución 109/2021, a Ministerio de Ambiente resolution) and its Art. 5 operative ban. Because the barrier is the agency's own classification and the absence of a formal domestication/captive-bred exception, the fix is administrative: Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021 contemplates regulated exceptions, and the directorate already exercises de-facto interpretive discretion by treating R. norvegicus as domestic. So there is no hostile statute to repeal and nothing to take to Congress — pushing the legislature would solve a problem that doesn't exist on paper. Federal-vs-provincial dimension: the federal government controls inter-provincial commerce, imports, and the EEI list, but the police power over the contents of a private home falls to provinces/municipalities, so even a favorable national clarification on tenencia would not bind a province that chooses to enact a stricter local ban — this is a federal-first ask whose protection is reinforced, not replaced, by keeping breeder/captive-origin paperwork.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente, Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible) (executive / agency) — rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar
    The national environmental Application Authority that maintains the EEI list (Res. 109/2021), enforces the Art. 5 prohibitions, runs the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021), and holds the pre-import authorization power over wildlife. It is the only office that can issue a written clarification on tenencia and grant or interpret an Art. 6 exception extending captive-bred R. rattus the de-facto domestic treatment already given to R. norvegicus. rpuofs@ambiente.gob.ar is the directorate's wildlife-operator inbox; mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar is the general entry desk. [Updated 2026-06-11: contact via rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar after the directorate's 2026-04-01 migration from @ambiente.gob.ar; mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar is dead (hard-bounce).]
  • SENASA — Dirección de Comercio Exterior Animal (Mascotas No Tradicionales) (executive / agency) — responde@senasa.gob.ar
    The national animal-health service that runs the import protocol for non-traditional pets (CVI, SIGTrámites/TAD). Sanitary clearance is subordinate to the environmental veto, so SENASA is the right office to ask whether an EEI-1 companion rodent is auto-rejected in TAD or whether a CVI can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen. responde@senasa.gob.ar is the confirmed general inbox; dcea@senasa.gob.ar reaches the foreign-animal-trade directorate.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

I am writing as a private hobbyist regarding the regulatory status of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as an indoor companion animal. I understand the species is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021, and that Article 5 prohibits its breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement.

I have two questions and one request for clarification.

First, on possession (tenencia): Article 5 enumerates the banned activities but does not include passive private possession. Could you confirm in writing that simply keeping a pre-existing, captive-bred R. rattus indoors — never released into the environment — is not among the activities prohibited by Article 5?

Second, on parity with the fancy rat: Rattus norvegicus carries the identical EEI-1 listing, yet its captive-bred laboratory and fancy strains are bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because they are treated in practice as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. This is consistent with how domestication is normally understood: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals, because what matters is domestication, not wild ancestry. The fancy rat earned that same recognition despite its wild origin. R. rattus born and raised in captivity to captive parents is, in every practical husbandry sense, indistinguishable from the fancy rat and equally non-releasable — domesticated on identical terms. Does any formal regulatory exception exist — via Article 6 of Resolución 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence — that could extend to documented, closed-colony, captive-bred R. rattus the same domestic-animal treatment already afforded de facto to R. norvegicus, so that such specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization and transport prohibitions?

I am asking purely to understand the regulatory framework and to keep any animal lawfully and responsibly. Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Español
A la Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

Me dirijo a ustedes como aficionado/a particular respecto de la situación regulatoria de la rata de techo (Rattus rattus) tenida como animal de compañía dentro del hogar. Entiendo que la especie está clasificada como Especie Exótica Invasora Categoría 1 (EEI-1) en el Anexo I de la Resolución 109/2021, y que su Artículo 5 prohíbe su cría, compra y venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional y movimiento interjurisdiccional.

Formulo dos consultas y una solicitud de aclaración.

Primero, sobre la tenencia: el Artículo 5 enumera las actividades prohibidas pero no incluye la tenencia o posesión particular pasiva. ¿Podrían confirmarme por escrito que la mera tenencia de un ejemplar de R. rattus ya existente, nacido en cautiverio y mantenido íntegramente en el interior de la vivienda —sin liberación al ambiente— no se encuentra entre las actividades prohibidas por el Artículo 5?

Segundo, sobre la paridad con la rata doméstica común: Rattus norvegicus figura con idéntica clasificación EEI-1, y sin embargo sus cepas de laboratorio y domésticas criadas en cautiverio se crían, transportan y venden abiertamente en todo el país porque, en la práctica, se las trata como animales domésticos fuera del régimen de fauna silvestre. Esto es coherente con cómo se entiende habitualmente la domesticación: el perro desciende del lobo y el gato de un félido silvestre, y no obstante ambos son reconocidos como animales domésticos, porque lo que importa es la domesticación y no el origen silvestre. La rata 'fancy' obtuvo ese mismo reconocimiento pese a su origen silvestre. Un ejemplar de R. rattus nacido y criado en cautiverio, hijo de padres también criados en cautiverio, es en todo sentido práctico de manejo indistinguible de la rata 'fancy' e igualmente no liberable — domesticado en idénticos términos. ¿Existe alguna excepción reglamentaria formal —vía Artículo 6 de la Resolución 109/2021, un dictamen interno o jurisprudencia administrativa— que pueda extender a los ejemplares documentados de R. rattus, de colonia cerrada y criados en cautiverio, el mismo tratamiento de 'animal doméstico' que de hecho ya se otorga a R. norvegicus, de modo que tales ejemplares queden fuera de las prohibiciones de comercialización y transporte propias de la categoría EEI-1?

Mi consulta tiene como único fin comprender el marco regulatorio y poder tener cualquier animal de manera lícita y responsable. Desde ya, agradezco su tiempo y orientación.

[Su nombre]
[Sus datos de contacto]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Australia

Summary. Australia is very restrictive. No exotic rodents may be imported as pets (only cats, dogs, rabbits, horses and certain birds can be imported), and the black rat (Rattus rattus) is a declared pest in parts of the country. Keeping a black rat as a pet is effectively prohibited or heavily restricted, and varies by state/territory.

Part confirmed, part preliminary — some activities below are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency; others we’re still verifying. Each section is labelled.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), Animal & Biological Imports Branch, written reply June 2026 (officer 'Mel'): live rats may be imported into Australia for laboratory purposes only; there are NO import conditions allowing rats as household pets, and 'there is currently no pathway to import Rattus rattus as a pet into Australia' (it is an introduced pest and not on the DCCEEW Live Import List). DAFF also confirmed that keeping, breeding, sale, and movement WITHIN Australia, and pest-species management, are regulated by STATE/TERRITORY governments — contact the relevant state/territory authority for those.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

The black rat is a declared/feral pest in parts of Australia (e.g., the Northern Territory), and exotic rodents are not approved as pets; domestic fancy rats (R. norvegicus) are the only commonly kept pet rat. Confirm per state/territory.

Sources: Australian Dept of Agriculture, Northern Territory Government

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding a declared pest species is restricted/prohibited under state biosecurity law.

Sources: Northern Territory Government

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling/trading a declared pest species is restricted/prohibited under state biosecurity law.

Sources: Northern Territory Government

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

AGENCY-CONFIRMED (DAFF, June 2026): there is currently NO pathway to import Rattus rattus into Australia as a pet — live rats may be imported for laboratory purposes only, and R. rattus (an introduced pest) has no biosecurity import conditions as a companion animal and is not on the DCCEEW Live Import List. Federal (Biosecurity Act 2015 + EPBC Act Live Import List).

Sources: Australian Dept of Agriculture

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Australia. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Australia

In Australia, you can legally keep the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus, the domesticated brown rat) as a pet in most states, but the roof rat / black rat (Rattus rattus) is treated very differently — not because tame, captive-bred roof rats behave like pests, but because of how two lists are written. (1) At the federal level, the only animals allowed to be imported as live pets are a short approved set (dogs, cats, rabbits, horses and certain birds); exotic rodents are simply not on the EPBC Act "Live Import List," so importing one is prohibited. (2) At the state/territory level, Rattus rattus is named on pest-animal declarations as a widespread "established invasive animal" (for example under the Northern Territory pest listing and Victoria's Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994 classifications). The result is that an animal kept as a beloved, indoor-only pet elsewhere in the world is, in Australia, defined by law as a pest species — even when the individual rat was bred in captivity, has never lived wild, and will never be released. The barrier here is the wording of the lists themselves, not an official misunderstanding them.

The ask: Australia's rules turn on lists, so the meaningful change is a change to those lists — and that goes through formal application and public-comment (rulemaking) channels, not a request for an official to "reinterpret." We ask supporters to: (1) write to the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW), which administers the EPBC Act Live Import List, to register interest in having domesticated/captive-bred rat lineages considered, and to watch and respond to the public "invitations to comment" when relevant species are proposed; and (2) raise the species-versus-domestication distinction with the relevant state/territory biosecurity authority and, ultimately, elected members, so any future review of pest-animal declarations distinguishes wild pest populations from tame, captive-bred companion animals kept strictly indoors. The specific change sought: recognise that captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus kept indoors as pets are not the wild pest the lists were written to control, and create a lawful pathway for them — the same way Rattus norvegicus is already kept as a pet. Two threads support this. First, domestication, not wild ancestry, is what the law already recognises elsewhere: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are domestic. Second, the underlying call is a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Australia and its states — the country already permits cats and dogs, themselves non-native and among the most documented killers of native and island wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth it, so the open question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats is outweighed by the same companionship benefit. We ask the decision-makers to weigh that narrow question, not to reach a particular result.

Where the lever really is: BRANCH (b): the problem is the LAW/LISTS AS WRITTEN, not a bureaucracy misreading them — so do NOT ask an agency to "reinterpret." Concretely for Australia, there are two written instruments and both correctly exclude/flag the species: (1) the EPBC Act Live Import List (administered by DCCEEW) is a positive list — only species ON it may be imported as pets, and exotic rodents including Rattus rattus are not on it; an official applying that list to refuse import is applying the law correctly. The only way it changes is a formal application to amend the Live Import List, which triggers a risk assessment and a public consultation window — i.e. rulemaking. (2) State/territory pest-animal declarations (e.g. NT pest listing; Victoria's prohibited/controlled/regulated/established classifications under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994) name Rattus rattus as an established invasive pest; an official applying that declaration is, again, applying the law correctly. Removing or carving an exemption out of a declaration requires changing the regulation/declaration, not a clarification letter. Therefore the lever is the rulemaking / public-comment process (DCCEEW Live Import List amendment + open invitations to comment) and, behind it, the minister/legislature who set these instruments — plus a longer-game appeal to state biosecurity bodies and elected members to distinguish wild pests from tame captive-bred pets. A polite letter to an agency inbox is still worth sending to register interest and seed a future review, but supporters should understand it will not by itself change a list the agency is correctly applying.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) — EPBC Act Live Import List / exotic species assessment (executive / agency) — exotic.species@dcceew.gov.au
    DCCEEW administers the federal positive list (the Live Import List under the EPBC Act) that determines which animals may be imported as pets — exotic rodents are not on it. This is the correct touchpoint to register interest in, and ask about, the formal process to amend the list. Changing the list, not reinterpreting it, is the real lever.
  • DCCEEW — Wildlife trade 'Invitations to comment' (public consultation portal) (public comment) — official contact page
    Amendments to the Live Import List go through a public-comment window. This is the official portal where open consultations are posted and the public can lodge submissions — the rulemaking channel where supporters' voices actually count. Watch it and respond when a relevant species is proposed.
  • Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) — Biosecurity import enquiries (executive / agency) — official contact page
    DAFF administers biosecurity import rules under the Biosecurity Act 2015. Use this official online enquiry form to ask about the lawful pathway (or current absence of one) for a domesticated rat and to register interest. Note: DAFF applies the import rules as written, so this seeds a future review rather than overriding the list.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Live Import List / exotic species team,

I am writing as a supporter of responsible, domesticated pet-rat keeping. In most Australian states people lawfully keep the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) as a gentle, family companion. I am asking that domesticated, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) be given a lawful pathway too.

My concern is with how the rules are written, not with how your team applies them. The roof rat is excluded from the Live Import List and is named on state pest declarations as a wild invasive animal. But the animals I am writing about are captive-bred, tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released — they are pets, not the wild pest those lists were designed to control. The distinction is species-versus-domestication: a domesticated lineage is not its wild relative, just as the pet fancy rat is already treated differently. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic because of generations bred for tameness — a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

I also recognise this is, in the end, a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Australia and its states. Australia permits cats and dogs — themselves non-native and among the most documented killers of native and island wildlife — because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, which would never be released, is outweighed by the companionship and public benefit they offer. I am not asking you to reach a particular result, only that any future review weigh that question rather than rest on the species' name alone.

Could you please tell me the current process to apply to amend the Live Import List, and how I can be notified of any public consultation relevant to domesticated rats? I would value the chance to make a submission.

Thank you for your time and for the opportunity to comment.

[Your name]
[Your suburb/state, Australia]
[Your email]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada

Summary. Canada has no single national rule for keeping a roof rat — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Alberta bans the entire genus Rattus outright (a famously 'rat-free' province); Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat on its captive-wildlife allowed list; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow it (BC under a tame-captive exemption, Quebec with an import notice that the fancy rat is exempt from). Federally, the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate as long as it does NOT come from Africa. Check your province (below) AND your municipality.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate the day-to-day keeping of companion animals — that is left entirely to the provinces and municipalities, and the answer changes drastically at provincial borders. Alberta PROHIBITS keeping any rat (genus Rattus) with no pet exemption; Saskatchewan EXPLICITLY allows the black rat as captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia allow it. So there is no single Canadian answer — see your province below.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated; follows provincial possession rules. Prohibited where keeping is banned (Alberta), legal where the species is allowed (SK/ON/QC/BC). Commercial breeders everywhere also face municipal business-licensing, zoning, and provincial animal-welfare standards.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated within Canada; follows provincial rules and municipal pet-shop / commercial-breeder licensing. Prohibited in Alberta (sale/distribution of a declared pest is banned); legal in SK/ON/QC/BC subject to local business rules.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Bringing a pet rat INTO Canada is permissive federally: the CFIA does not require an import permit or veterinary health certificate for pet rodents — you simply declare the animal to the Canada Border Services Agency. The big exceptions: any rodent originating from the continent of Africa is barred (plague/monkeypox rule), airlines may demand their own vet certificate, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union is currently suspended. Critically, your destination PROVINCE's rules still apply — you may not bring a rat into (or, arguably, through) Alberta at all.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA, CFIA

Restrictions & responsibilities

Federal import is permit-free for pet rodents NOT from Africa — but a Rattus rattus originating from any African country is barred entry (and may be seized or destroyed). Airlines often require a veterinary health certificate even though the government does not, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) is suspended until further notice.
  • Declare the animal as a pet to the CBSA at the border
  • Confirm it is not African-origin
  • Check your airline's own health-certificate rule

Forms: Bringing animals to Canada — CFIA · Where: Canada Border Services Agency / CFIA National Import Service Centre · Fees: No CFIA fee for pet rodents

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA

The answer depends entirely on your province. Alberta bans all rats (do NOT bring one in); Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia permit them. Always check your province (below) and your municipal bylaws (which can cap the number of animals or require a breeder licence).
  • Find your province below
  • Check your city/municipal animal bylaws

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Canada

Canada has no single national rule for keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat as allowed captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all permit it; and federally the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate (the one hard exception: no rodents originating from Africa). The outlier — and the one true prohibition in Canada — is Alberta. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and its Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a "declared pest," and the Government of Alberta states plainly that "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." There is no exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept indoors as a companion. The rule was written to protect Alberta's celebrated rat-free farmland from wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) establishing breeding colonies, but as written it sweeps in domesticated pet rats that pose none of that agricultural risk and have never founded a wild population.

The ask: Ask Alberta to add a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred companion rats kept indoors — the same kind of carve-out that lets neighbouring provinces allow them safely. The case rests on a cost-benefit judgment that is Alberta's to make: the province already permits cats and dogs, themselves non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off, so the open question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats (which have never founded a wild colony) is outweighed by the same companionship benefit — a question to put to the decision-makers, not a conclusion to assert. The change is to the regulation itself (a job for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation and your MLA), not a favour the rat-control program can grant on its own, because the program is correctly applying the law as written. Where you live OUTSIDE Alberta, no change is needed to keep a pet roof rat — just confirm your province's rule and your municipal bylaws.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the LAW AS WRITTEN. The barrier is a deliberate statutory/regulatory listing, not a clerk's misreading. Alberta's Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, made under the Agricultural Pests Act, declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and the Government of Alberta's own rat-control page states "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta" with no pet exemption. The rat-control program is applying that regulation exactly as drafted — so emailing the program to ask permission, or appealing its decision, will NOT work, because there is nothing for it to reinterpret. The fix is to amend the regulation to add a captive-bred companion-animal exemption, which is a decision for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation (the regulation is set by the Minister/Cabinet) acting on public and political input. The correct lever is therefore the legislature: your MLA and the Minister, who can champion or direct a regulatory amendment. (For the other relevant provinces — SK, ON, QC, BC — there is no law-as-written problem to fix; the roof rat is already permitted, so they are not advocacy targets, only a "confirm-your-province" check.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Members of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta — official MLA directory / 'find your MLA' (legislature) — official contact page
    The prohibition lives in a regulation the Minister and Cabinet control, so the change must come through the political/legislative branch. This official Legislative Assembly page lets any Alberta resident look up and contact their own MLA — the representative who can raise a regulatory amendment or relay constituent demand to the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation. Use it to write your own MLA; never address an individual member by name picked at random.
  • Elections Alberta — Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) search (legislature) — official contact page
    An independent official tool to confirm which MLA represents your address, in case you are unsure of your constituency before contacting them via the Assembly directory above.
  • Alberta Rat Control Program (Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation) — official program inbox (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Secondary channel. This is the official inbox of the program that administers the declared-pest rule. It cannot grant a pet exemption on its own (the regulation must change first), but a polite written request for the government's current position on tame captive-bred companion rats, and for whether a narrow exemption could be recommended to the Minister, puts the ask on record with the administering body and can be cited when you write your MLA. Verified on the Government of Alberta rat-control program page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To my MLA / the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation,

I am writing about Alberta's prohibition on keeping pet rats. Under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred companion rat is illegal to own here.

I understand and support the goal: keeping wild Norway rats from establishing in Alberta's farmland. But the regulation as written also bans domesticated pet rats that are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released — animals that pose none of the agricultural risk the rule was designed to stop, and that have never founded a wild colony.

Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow these pets safely. The issue is not whether a rat can be domesticated — it plainly can: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic because of generations bred for tameness, and the captive-bred pet rat is no different. The issue is simply that the species is on a list with no exemption for companion animals.

Ultimately this is a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Alberta. The province already permits cats and dogs — themselves non-native animals well documented to kill native wildlife — because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is outweighed by the companionship they offer. I am not asking you to reach a particular conclusion — only to weigh that question, which neighbouring provinces have already answered by allowing these pets while keeping their own wild-rat controls in place.

I respectfully ask you to support adding a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred rats kept indoors as pets, while leaving the wild-rat controls fully in place.

Thank you for considering this.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town and constituency]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Spain

Summary. Earlier research wrongly treated the roof rat as banned nationwide; the environment ministry has now corrected that. On the Spanish mainland (and everywhere outside the Canary Islands) Rattus rattus is NOT a cataloged invasive species, so the Real Decreto 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not apply there — keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023) and its forthcoming companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list), which is still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS listed in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras for that territory alone, so there the Art. 7.1 ban (possess/breed/sell/transport live specimens) does apply. Commercial breeding or sale anywhere in Spain requires a núcleo zoológico (establishment) authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma, and animal health/identification/movement of bred or traded animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. So the country-level reality is split: not prohibited on the mainland (welfare-regulated, positive list pending) but cataloged-and-prohibited in the Canaries.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Spain's environment ministry for ecological transition (biodiversity mailbox), written reply June 2026, corrected the prior nationwide-ban reading: Rattus rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras EXCLUSIVELY for the case of the Canary Islands, not nationwide. The ministry also set out the competence split: invasive-species catalogues and exotic/wildlife matters sit with the environment ministry (natural heritage and biodiversity); the animal-welfare framework for companion animals is Ley 7/2023, with competence mainly at the social-rights/consumer ministry (which is also building the companion-animal positive list); animal health, identification, movement, and the sanitary conditions of breeding, trade and transport sit with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food; and authorization of núcleos zoológicos, breeding centres and establishment registries sits with the Comunidades Autónomas (regional governments). The practical effect: on the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the Art. 7.1 ban does not reach it and keeping is permissible under the general welfare law pending the positive list; in the Canary Islands it is cataloged and the Art. 7.1 ban applies.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the Spanish mainland (and outside the Canary Islands), R. rattus is NOT in the Catálogo Español de EEI, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession ban does not apply and keeping is not prohibited; it is instead governed by the general animal-welfare framework of Ley 7/2023, with the companion-animal positive list still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS cataloged, so there Art. 7.1 prohibits possession of live specimens. The country-level reality is therefore 'legal on the mainland, prohibited in the Canaries'; confidence is medium because the forthcoming positive list could change mainland keepability once it takes effect.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, MITECO, BOE / Gobierno de España

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 breeding ban does not apply there; breeding for sale or as an establishment requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma (the regional government that authorizes breeding centres and establishment registries), and animal health/identification of bred animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Canary Islands, where R. rattus IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits reproduction of live specimens, so breeding there is barred. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (regional núcleo-zoológico authorization on the mainland); confidence medium pending the positive-list outcome.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 trade/commerce ban does not apply there; selling or commercially supplying live animals requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the Comunidad Autónoma, with animal-health/identification/movement conditions under the Ministry of Agriculture, and welfare/transfer requirements under Ley 7/2023. In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'tráfico y comercio de ejemplares vivos,' so sale/transfer there is barred. Private free rehoming on the mainland is not banned but is subject to the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; commercial sale needs the establishment authorization — hence legal_with_permit at country level.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 transport ban does not apply there; movement of bred or traded animals is instead subject to the animal-health, identification and sanitary-movement rules administered by the Ministry of Agriculture (and ordinary welfare-in-transport requirements). In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'transporte' of live specimens. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no EU-level border ban; non-commercial pet movement within the EU follows Reg. (EU) 576/2013, but the Canary-Islands catalogue prohibition takes effect on Canarian soil. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (sanitary/movement conditions on the mainland); never release.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Territorial split. CANARY ISLANDS: R. rattus is a cataloged invasive species (RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1), so possessing, breeding, selling/giving or transporting a live one is prohibited there. MAINLAND (and elsewhere outside the Canaries): R. rattus is NOT cataloged, so it is not banned — keeping is governed by Ley 7/2023 (welfare; companion-animal positive list still pending/not in force), commercial breeding or sale needs a Comunidad-Autónoma núcleo zoológico authorization, and animal health/identification/movement fall under the Ministry of Agriculture. Never release anywhere.
  • Mainland: keep under the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; watch for the forthcoming companion-animal positive list
  • Mainland commercial breeding/sale: obtain a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma; meet Ministry of Agriculture animal-health/movement rules
  • Canary Islands: do not acquire, breed, sell or move R. rattus (cataloged invasive, Art. 7.1 ban)
  • If advocating: ask the positive-list rulemaking ministry to include captive-bred R. rattus; for the Canaries, the formal exclusión/de-cataloguing procedure

Where: Comunidad Autónoma (núcleo zoológico authorization); environment ministry — biodiversity (Catálogo de EEI / Canaries de-cataloguing); social-rights/consumer ministry (positive list)

Source: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Help change this

How to help in Spain

Spain's picture for the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is territorial, not a blanket ban — a point the environment ministry confirmed in writing in June 2026. The species is written into the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Real Decreto 630/2013) ONLY for the Canary Islands; on the mainland and elsewhere it is not a cataloged invasive species, so the Article 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not reach it there. Mainland keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023), under which the companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list) of species that may be kept as pets is still being written and is not yet in force. The live concern is what happens when that list takes effect: the law generally excludes catalogue-listed invasive species from the positive list, and because R. rattus is cataloged in one territory (the Canaries) it is an awkward edge case — a captive-bred domestic line that is perfectly legal to keep on the mainland today could be left off the national positive list by default unless the rulemaking treats it deliberately. So the barrier is not a current prohibition; it is the risk that a future list quietly closes the door that is open today.

The ask: Ask the ministry responsible for the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (social-rights/consumer) to ensure captive-bred Rattus rattus is INCLUDED on the listado positivo — or, failing inclusion, handled through registration and welfare conditions — so that a species which is lawful to keep on the mainland today remains keepable once the list takes effect. Concretely, ask the rulemaking to address the partially-cataloged edge case explicitly: because R. rattus is cataloged only for the Canary Islands and is not an invasive species on the mainland, its captive-bred, indoor, never-released lineages should not be swept out of the national positive list by the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion, which was designed for species cataloged across Spain. In weighing the invasive-species worry that underlies that exclusion, invite the ministry to consider the question as a cost-benefit one that is Spain's to decide: the cat and the dog are themselves non-native across most of Spain and are documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet they are permitted everywhere because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off — so the fair question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is outweighed by the companionship and public benefit they offer. We do not ask the ministry to disregard its ecological concerns or to reach a particular result; we ask it to weigh this narrow question and decide. Separately, for keepers in the Canary Islands, ask the environment ministry about the formal exclusión (de-cataloguing) procedure under Article 64 of Ley 42/2007 and RD 630/2013 to remove captive-origin R. rattus from the catalogue for that territory.

Where the lever really is: Two distinct, correct levers — pick by territory and by question. (1) POSITIVE LIST = a RULEMAKING lever at the social-rights/consumer ministry (Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales), which owns the Ley 7/2023 'listado positivo' royal decree still in progress. The ask is inclusion of captive-bred R. rattus, with explicit treatment of the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries, not on the mainland). This is the primary lever because mainland keeping is otherwise already lawful and the only real future risk is exclusion-by-default from the positive list. (2) CANARY-ISLANDS DE-CATALOGUING = an AGENCY-PROCEDURE lever at the environment ministry (which owns the Catálogo de EEI). The formal exclusión procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation with scientific justification and is the route to lift the Art. 7.1 ban for the Canaries; it is secondary because it only matters for keepers in that territory. Authorization of breeding/sale establishments (núcleos zoológicos) is a separate Comunidad-Autónoma matter, and animal health/movement sits with the Ministry of Agriculture — neither is an advocacy barrier, just the ordinary permitting layer. There is NO front-desk 'clarification' that changes any of this, and the prior positive-list public-comment window is closed, so route the positive-list ask through the rulemaking ministry's mailbox (and consider a keeper-rights ally to carry the scientific case).

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030 — Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ley 7/2023 listado positivo rulemaking) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the ministry writing the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list — the instrument that will decide, going forward, whether captive-bred R. rattus may be kept as a pet on the mainland once the list is in force. It is the correct office to ask that captive-bred R. rattus be INCLUDED on the positive list and that the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries) be resolved deliberately rather than by the default 'no catálogo species' exclusion. The prior public-comment window (17 Apr – 8 May 2026) is closed, so engage via the ministry's published rulemaking channel rather than as an open consultation.
  • Environment ministry — biodiversity sub-directorate (Catálogo Español de EEI): exclusión / de-cataloguing procedure for the Canary Islands listing (executive / agency) — buzon-sgb@miteco.es
    This office owns the invasive-species catalogue and confirmed in June 2026 that R. rattus is cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands. Its formal 'Catalogación o descatalogación de taxones' procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation to request exclusión (de-listing) with scientific justification. This is the correct lever ONLY for the Canaries, where the Art. 7.1 ban actually applies — it is irrelevant on the mainland, where the species is not cataloged.
  • Federación FAUNA — keeper/breeder rights federation (advocacy ally, not a government body) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Spain's principal keeper/breeder federation, active in the listado-positivo rulemaking. As an organisation it can carry the scientific/husbandry case for INCLUDING captive-bred R. rattus on the positive list (and, for Canaries keepers, a de-cataloguing petition) more effectively than a lone keeper. Engage as an ally to the rulemaking ask, not as a substitute for it. (Do NOT route this to the conservation-aligned Coalición para el Listado Positivo.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Re: Treatment of captive-bred Rattus rattus in the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (listado positivo)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing as a member of the public who cares about the welfare of domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus). I understand from the environment ministry that R. rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras only for the case of the Canary Islands, and is not a cataloged invasive species on the mainland — where keeping it is currently governed by Ley 7/2023 rather than by any catalogue ban.

My concern is the forthcoming companion-animal positive list. Because the law generally excludes catalogue-listed species from the positive list, a species that is cataloged in only one territory (the Canary Islands) risks being left off the national list by default, even though on the mainland it is not an invasive species and is lawful to keep today.

I would respectfully ask: (1) that captive-bred Rattus rattus be INCLUDED on the listado positivo, so that a domesticated, indoor, never-released line that is keepable on the mainland today remains keepable once the list is in force; and (2) that the rulemaking address the partial-catalogue situation explicitly, distinguishing the Canary-Islands listing from mainland status, rather than applying the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion to a species that is invasive in only one region. If full inclusion is not possible, please advise whether captive-bred lineages could instead be handled through registration and welfare conditions.

Where the worry is the species' invasive potential, I would ask you to weigh this as a cost-benefit question that is Spain's to decide. Cats and dogs are themselves non-native across most of Spain and are well documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet they are permitted everywhere because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The fair question is therefore whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is outweighed by the companionship and public benefit they bring. I am not asking the ministry to disregard its ecological concerns or to reach any particular outcome — only to weigh this specific, narrowly-conditioned question and decide.

Thank you for your time and for your work on animal welfare.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town / province]
[Date]
Español
A: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Asunto: Tratamiento de la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad en el listado positivo de animales de compañía de la Ley 7/2023

Estimados señores:

Les escribo como ciudadano preocupado por el bienestar de las ratas domésticas (Rattus rattus). Según me ha indicado el ministerio competente en medio ambiente, la R. rattus está incluida en el Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras únicamente para el caso de las Islas Canarias, y no es especie catalogada invasora en la península, donde su tenencia se rige por la Ley 7/2023 y no por ninguna prohibición del Catálogo.

Mi preocupación es el futuro listado positivo de animales de compañía. Dado que la ley excluye con carácter general del listado positivo a las especies catalogadas, una especie catalogada en un solo territorio (las Islas Canarias) corre el riesgo de quedar fuera del listado nacional por defecto, pese a que en la península no es una especie invasora y hoy su tenencia es lícita.

Les ruego respetuosamente: (1) que la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad se INCLUYA en el listado positivo, de modo que un linaje doméstico, mantenido en el interior del hogar y nunca liberado, que hoy puede tenerse en la península, siga pudiendo mantenerse cuando el listado entre en vigor; y (2) que el desarrollo reglamentario aborde de forma expresa la situación de catalogación parcial, distinguiendo la inclusión en Canarias del estatus peninsular, en lugar de aplicar la exclusión general de 'especies catalogadas' a una especie que es invasora en una sola región. Si la inclusión plena no fuera posible, les ruego me indiquen si los linajes criados en cautividad podrían regularse mediante registro y condiciones de bienestar.

Cuando la preocupación sea el potencial invasor de la especie, les ruego que lo valoren como una cuestión de coste-beneficio que corresponde decidir a España. El gato y el perro son también especies no autóctonas en casi toda España y está bien documentado que perjudican a la fauna autóctona, en especial a la insular, y sin embargo se permiten en todas partes porque se considera que su compañía compensa ese coste. La pregunta justa es, por tanto, si el limitado riesgo adicional de unas pocas ratas domésticas esterilizadas o alteradas, dóciles y mantenidas siempre en interior queda compensado por la compañía y el beneficio público que aportan. No les pido que ignoren sus preocupaciones ecológicas ni que lleguen a un resultado concreto, sino únicamente que valoren esta cuestión específica y acotada y decidan.

Les agradezco su tiempo y la labor que realizan en favor del bienestar animal.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su localidad / provincia]
[Fecha]
