item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › France

Summary. In France the roof rat falls on the wrong side of a purely taxonomic line. The official domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of Rattus norvegicus among the Muridae — so Rattus rattus is legally 'non-domestic,' which pulls it into the Code de l'environnement's regime for espèces non domestiques. In practice a hobbyist with a small number of captive-bred roof rats must file a prefectural déclaration de détention (but not the harder certificat de capacité, which only kicks in above ~40 adult mammals), register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer. The good news: R. rattus is NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) or France's metropolitan invasive Arrêté, so there's no keeping/sale ban. The wrinkle: the 2021 animal-welfare law created a 'positive list' for pet species (Art. L413-1A) that, as of 2026, still hasn't been published — leaving the regime in limbo and opening a concrete advocacy window to request R. rattus's inclusion.

Preliminary — built from official sources but not yet agency-confirmed; a solid starting point. Know the local rule? Tell us.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is non-domestic (only R. norvegicus strains are on the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 domestic list), so it's governed by Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 et seq. + the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 (mod. 5 sept. 2025). Below the threshold (generally ~40 adult mammals) a hobbyist needs only a prefectural déclaration de détention — not a certificat de capacité — filed before acquisition, plus I-FAP registration. Not banned (R. rattus absent from the EU Union list + metropolitan invasive Arrêté). ⚠️ The 2021 positive-list (L413-1A) is still unpublished as of 2026, so the pre-existing declaration regime continues.

Sources: Ministère de l'Écologie, Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Hobby breeding (élevage d'agrément) extends detention: below the certificat-de-capacité threshold (~40 adult mammals) only the prefectural déclaration de détention is required; above it, a certificat de capacité (Art. L413-2) and possibly an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement (Art. L413-3) apply. No specific ban on breeding captive R. rattus. The L413-1A 'élevage de conservation' carve-out awaits its implementing decree.

Sources: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Transfer of a non-domestic animal is legal but procedural: an attestation de cession (two copies) under Art. R413-1 et seq. + registration of each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days of acquisition. A private person may give animals away but cannot sell commercially to the public without being a declared pet-trade establishment (animalerie) under Code rural Art. L214-6. No EU sale ban (R. rattus not on the Union list).

Sources: Légifrance, Légifrance, EU / EUR-Lex

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents has no EU passport/health-certificate scheme like cats/dogs, but the French déclaration de détention + I-FAP registration must be satisfied; an attestation de cession is needed if ownership changes. IMPORT from a non-EU country requires a veterinary health certificate per the Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 model for rodents), limited to 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so no import ban. ⚠️ French OVERSEAS territories (Réunion, Martinique, Polynésie) actively manage R. rattus as invasive — local rules there may restrict.

Sources: Ministère de l'Agriculture, EU / EUR-Lex, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is 'non-domestic' in France, file a prefectural déclaration de détention BEFORE acquiring one (online or registered mail) and register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days. A certificat de capacité is only required above the ~40-adult-mammal threshold. Keep the paperwork — it's the difference between a legal hobby and an offence.
  • File a déclaration de détention with the préfecture (DDT/DREAL) before acquisition
  • Register each animal in I-FAP within 8 days of acquisition

Forms: Déclaration de détention d'animaux non domestiques · Where: Préfecture de département (DDT/DREAL); I-FAP

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Importing from outside the EU needs a veterinary health certificate (Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002, Annexe 18 model for rodents), max 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. French overseas territories manage R. rattus as invasive — check local prefectoral rules there. Never release a roof rat.

Source: Ministère de l'Agriculture

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in France
Time-sensitive: The implementing arrêté establishing the Art. L413-1A "positive list" of non-domestic companion species is still unpublished as of late 2025 (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, awaiting government reply; an April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report recommended publishing it and assigning coordination to ANSES). This means the list is being prepared now — the moment to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion is BEFORE the arrêté is finalized. No specific public-comment window for this arrêté is open at the time of writing; watch the official public-consultation portal (consultations-publiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr, "Eau et biodiversité") for the draft to appear.

In France the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is treated differently from the ordinary fancy rat purely because of taxonomy, not because of how the animal lives. The official list of domestic animals (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, among the rodents. Because the roof rat is a different species, it is classified as "non-domestic" — even when it is captive-bred, hand-tame, and has never lived in the wild. That single taxonomic line pulls a tame pet rat into the framework for non-domestic species under the Code de l'environnement: before you acquire one you must file a prefectural déclaration de détention, register each animal in the national I-FAP file within eight days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer — paperwork a fancy-rat keeper never touches. Separately, the 2021 animal-welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created a forthcoming "positive list" of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals, but the implementing arrêté still has not been published (confirmed by a November 2025 Sénat written question). That leaves the regime in limbo — and it means captive-bred Rattus rattus could be silently left off the list when it is finally drawn up.

The ask: Ask the Ministre chargé de l'environnement (the minister who, under Art. L413-1A, fixes the positive list) to formally examine captive-bred, indoor-kept Rattus rattus for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic companion species — so that a tame, captive-bred roof rat is treated like the fancy rat it resembles in every practical way, rather than carrying declaration and registration burdens based only on its Latin name. Make the point that domestication, not wild ancestry, is what the law should weigh: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are universally recognised as domestic animals because generations of captive breeding for tameness — not the species label — is what defines a domestic animal, and a captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated in exactly that sense. Anyone may make this request in writing under Art. L413-1A, and the minister owes a reasoned reply within six months. When the draft arrêté goes out for public comment, also submit a short contribution on the official public-consultation portal supporting the species' inclusion.

Where the lever really is: This is the LEGISLATURE/RULEMAKING-WINDOW branch, not the bureaucracy-misreading branch — and the distinction matters concretely. The agencies (préfecture, OFB) are correctly applying the law: the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 genuinely lists only Rattus norvegicus strains as domestic, so a préfet who classes Rattus rattus as "non-domestic" and asks for a déclaration de détention is doing exactly what the texts require. Writing to OFB or your préfecture to complain will NOT change this — they cannot rewrite a national list, and they are not misapplying anything. The fix lives at the rulemaking level. France's own 2021 welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created the proper lever: a forthcoming "positive list" of non-domestic species allowed as companion animals, fixed by an arrêté of the minister responsible for the environment. Crucially, Art. L413-1A expressly invites "toute personne physique ou morale" to request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned ministerial answer due within six months and judicial review available. Because that implementing arrêté is still unpublished (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, still awaiting answer; April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report urged publication and ANSES coordination), there is a live, statutorily-invited window to get captive-bred Rattus rattus written ONTO the list before it is finalized — and to avoid a de-facto ban if the species is omitted. So the target is the Ministry (which holds the pen on the arrêté) via the formal L413-1A inclusion request, plus the official public-consultation portal when the draft arrêté is posted. This is not an individual representative matter, because the underlying statute already exists; what is missing and contestable is the executive instrument (the arrêté) and the species' place on it.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministère de la Transition écologique, de la Biodiversité, de la Forêt, de la Mer et de la Pêche — official contact portal (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This ministry holds the pen on the Art. L413-1A positive-list arrêté (the minister 'chargé de l'environnement' fixes the list). Under L413-1A any person may request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned reply due within six months. This is the official, secure electronic contact form (FranceConnect or email identification; acknowledgment within 10 business days). Address the request to the Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité (DEB).
  • Consultations publiques du ministère de la Transition écologique — rubrique « Eau et biodiversité » (public comment) — official contact page
    The official portal where draft arrêtés on water and biodiversity (including, when posted, the L413-1A positive-list arrêté) are opened for public comment. Submit a short contribution supporting inclusion of captive-bred Rattus rattus when the draft appears. No relevant window is open right now — monitor this page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request under Article L413-1A to examine captive-bred Rattus rattus for the positive list

To the Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

I am writing about the legal status of the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). Today it is classed as a non-domestic species only because the domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 August 2006) names just Rattus norvegicus among rodents. As a result, a captive-bred, hand-tame roof rat carries declaration and I-FAP registration burdens that an identical fancy rat never does — a difference based solely on the animal's Latin name, with no ecological rationale for animals that are bred in captivity, kept indoors, and never released.

Under Article L413-1A of the Code de l'environnement, I respectfully request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals.

These animals are captive-bred, tame, kept exclusively indoors, and never released into the wild. I ask that the species be treated like the domestic fancy rat it resembles in every practical respect. I would add that wild ancestry alone should not decide the question: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised everywhere as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness rather than its Latin name. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

Thank you for your consideration. I would be grateful for your reasoned reply within the six-month period provided by Article L413-1A.

[Your name]
[Town / department]
[Date]
Français
Objet: Demande au titre de l'article L413-1A d'examen du Rattus rattus né en captivité en vue de la liste positive

À l'attention de la Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

Je me permets de vous saisir au sujet du statut juridique du rat des toits de compagnie (Rattus rattus). Il est aujourd'hui classé parmi les espèces non domestiques au seul motif que la liste des animaux domestiques (arrêté du 11 août 2006) ne mentionne, parmi les rongeurs, que le Rattus norvegicus. De ce fait, un rat des toits né en captivité et apprivoisé entraîne des obligations de déclaration de détention et d'enregistrement I-FAP qu'un rat domestique identique n'impose jamais — une différence fondée sur le seul nom latin de l'animal, sans justification écologique pour des animaux nés en captivité, détenus en intérieur et jamais relâchés.

En application de l'article L413-1A du code de l'environnement, je sollicite respectueusement l'examen de l'inscription du Rattus rattus né en captivité sur la future liste positive des espèces non domestiques pouvant être détenues comme animaux de compagnie.

Ces animaux sont nés en captivité, apprivoisés, détenus exclusivement en intérieur et jamais relâchés dans la nature. Je demande que l'espèce soit traitée comme le rat domestique auquel elle ressemble en tout point sur le plan pratique. J'ajoute que la seule ascendance sauvage ne devrait pas trancher la question: le chien descend du loup et le chat d'un félidé sauvage, et pourtant tous deux sont partout reconnus comme des animaux domestiques, car ce qui définit un animal domestique, ce sont des générations d'élevage en captivité pour l'apprivoisement, et non son nom latin. Un rat des toits né en captivité est domestiqué exactement en ce sens.

Je vous remercie de votre attention et vous saurais gré de bien vouloir m'adresser une réponse motivée dans le délai de six mois prévu par l'article L413-1A.

[Votre nom]
[Commune / département]
[Date]

  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 — règles générales de détention d'animaux d'espèces non domestiques (Annexe 2 thresholds; mod. Arrêté du 5 sept. 2025) — Ministère de la Transition écologique

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Kingdom

Summary. In Great Britain, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal — it's omitted from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 and from the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 possession bans. BUT the roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981, so it's a strict-liability criminal offence to release it or let it escape into the wild (use escape-proof caging; you may not release a trapped one). Commercial breeding/selling needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (and inspectors may treat it as a non-domestic species). Sale is OUTRIGHT PROHIBITED in Northern Ireland (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A). Importing one is excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme and needs an APHA rabies import licence (Form RM01) + up to 4 months quarantine.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No statute bans mere possession of a captive-bred roof rat: the genus Rattus (family Muridae) is absent from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 schedule, it's not under the Destructive Imported Animals Act 1932, and it's not on Schedule 2 of the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 (the possession-ban list). Owners owe the Animal Welfare Act 2006 duty of care. Because R. rattus IS on Schedule 9 of the WCA 1981, releasing it or letting it escape is a criminal offence — and a trapped one may not be released back to the wild.

Sources: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk, UK Government / Defra, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Purely private, non-commercial hobby breeding is unregulated (no statutory litter limits), subject to the Animal Welfare Act 2006. The moment it becomes commercial (profit intent, >£1,000/yr gross from animal sales, dealing, or systematic advertising of litters), it requires a local-authority Animal Welfare licence under the Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regulations 2018 (England) / 2021 (Wales & Scotland). Never let breeding stock escape (Sch. 9).

Sources: Defra / local authorities, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

GREAT BRITAIN: selling as a business needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (the 'business test' / £1,000 HMRC trading allowance); inspectors may classify the roof rat under 'Part I — other non-domestic mammals' (higher burden, invasive-species containment) rather than 'Part H — domestic small rodents'. Giving one away free is generally outside the commercial 'sale' test. NORTHERN IRELAND: selling, offering for sale, or transporting for sale is an OUTRIGHT CRIMINAL OFFENCE (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A; R. rattus is on Sch. 9 Part 1) — no licensing pathway exists; even advertising is barred.

Sources: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC: legal under the Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006 — but use gnaw-proof, escape-proof carriers, because an escape in transit is a strict-liability offence (WCA 1981 s.14/Sch. 9). IMPORT: the roof rat is a rabies-susceptible non-native mammal EXCLUDED from the Pet Travel Scheme; you must apply for an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — non-EU origin means up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may be exempt if captive-bred/kept since birth. Northern Ireland adds Windsor-Framework pre-notification. No CITES permit (not endangered).

Sources: APHA / UK Government, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981: it is a criminal offence (strict liability — intent doesn't matter) to release it or allow it to escape into the wild anywhere in the UK. Use secure, gnaw-proof caging; a trapped/escaped roof rat may NOT be released — only humane options or an exceptional licence apply.

Source: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

In Great Britain, commercial breeding/selling (profit, >£1,000/yr, dealing, or systematic advertising) requires a local-authority Animal Welfare Activity Licence; expect possible 'Part I (non-domestic mammal)' treatment with specialist-knowledge + invasive-species containment requirements. In Northern Ireland, sale is prohibited entirely.
  • GB: apply to your local council for an Animal Activity Licence if you cross the business threshold
  • NI: do not sell/offer/transport-for-sale (Art. 15A)

Where: Local authority (GB); n/a (NI — prohibited) · Fees: Set by local authority

Source: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Importing a roof rat needs an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — it's excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme. Non-EU origin = up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may qualify for exemption if captive-bred and kept since birth. Apply to APHA Centre for International Trade (Carlisle) at least 4 weeks ahead.
  • Apply for APHA Form RM01 at least 4 weeks before import
  • Provide captive-bred-since-birth evidence to seek a quarantine exemption (EU origin)

Forms: APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) · Where: APHA Centre for International Trade, Carlisle · Fees: Quarantine at owner's expense

Source: APHA / UK Government

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Japan

Summary. In Japan, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated federally: the species is deliberately NOT a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物, hazardous) and NOT a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物) — a 2005 expert committee chose to exclude it because it's too long-established to regulate. Commercial activity (breeding for profit, retail sale, exhibition, or large-scale free rehoming) triggers registration as a First-Class (or Second-Class) Animal Handling Business with facility/welfare standards. The big restriction is IMPORT: bringing a roof rat into Japan is de-facto prohibited for the public — the Ministry of Health requires imported rodents to have lived since birth in a foreign-government-designated biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders don't qualify). Never release one.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private possession needs no federal permit: R. rattus is not a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物 — that list targets primates, big carnivores, large/venomous reptiles, not rodents), and it is not a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物). The 2005 Ministry of the Environment expert committee deliberately excluded it (long-established via maritime trade; eradication-vs-pet distinction). Domestic keeping is treated like keeping a fancy rat or guinea pig.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private breeding without intent to profit/advertise/distribute commercially is entirely outside the commercial animal-handling law. (Commercial-scale breeding triggers First-Class Animal Handling Business registration — see sell_give.)

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Selling for profit (or breeding to sell) requires registration as a First-Class Animal Handling Business (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture, plus facility/caging/disclosure standards and an Animal Handling Manager. Giving animals away free to 'a large number of unspecified people' on a continuing basis requires Second-Class (第二種) notification. Occasional free rehoming to friends/family is unregulated.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC transport between prefectures is unregulated (subject only to carrier policies). IMPORT is de-facto prohibited for pets: under the Infectious Diseases Control Law's Animal Import Notification System, all live rodents need a health certificate from the EXPORTING government certifying the animal lived since birth in a government-designated disease-free facility — which homes and hobby breeders cannot obtain, so a pet roof rat cannot legally be imported. (R. rattus is not on the absolute-prohibition list, but the facility rule is an effective ban.) Export from Japan is legal with the destination country's health certificate (MAFF AQS). Never release.

Sources: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial selling/breeding (for profit) = First-Class Animal Handling Business registration (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture: facility floor plans, cleanable escape-resistant enclosures, space to 'stand/lie/move' naturally, an Animal Handling Manager, and written species/sex/origin disclosure at transfer. Large-scale non-commercial giveaway = Second-Class (第二種) notification (penalty up to ¥300,000 for failing to notify).
  • Register as a First-Class Animal Handling Business before any commercial sale/breeding
  • Or file a Second-Class notification for large-scale free rehoming

Where: Prefectural government (animal welfare center / public health dept)

Source: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Importing a roof rat into Japan is effectively impossible for pet owners: imported rodents need an exporting-government health certificate proving the animal lived since birth in a government-DESIGNATED biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders can't qualify). MHLW states such pets 'basically cannot be brought into Japan.'

Where: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (quarantine station at port of entry)

Source: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Netherlands

Summary. Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands keeps a 'positive list' (huis- en hobbydierenlijst) of mammals that may be kept, bred, or sold without a permit. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is on it, but the black rat (Rattus rattus) is NOT, so keeping, breeding, importing, or trading black rats as pets is not permitted. A clear advocacy case to add the species.

Preliminary — built from official sources but not yet agency-confirmed; a solid starting point. Know the local rule? Tell us.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Only the ~30 mammal species on the positive list (huis- en hobbydierenlijst, in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept; the brown rat is listed but the black rat is not, so keeping it is not permitted.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be bred by private keepers.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be bought, sold, or freely traded by private individuals.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be imported by private keepers.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Netherlands. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Netherlands

Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands has used a "positive list" for mammals — the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. You may only keep, breed, buy or sell a mammal species if it is ON that list. The list was built by scientifically assessing more than 300 species. The brown/fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica) IS on the list, so keeping domesticated brown rats is fully legal. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) is NOT on the list, so under the current rules a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat may not legally be kept, bred, or rehomed in the Netherlands. The barrier here is not an agency misreading the law — the law genuinely does not (yet) include this species. The legal framework is the Wet dieren and the Besluit houders van dieren, administered by RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) with enforcement by the NVWA.

The ask: Ask RVO to assess the domesticated black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus, kept-strain) for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, using the official assessment procedure. The Dutch positive-list system has a built-in legal pathway: any interested party can submit an assessment request ("beoordeling aanvragen") for an unlisted mammal species through Mijn RVO. The fancy brown rat is already on the list, which establishes that a domesticated Rattus species can meet the welfare criteria; the request is that the closely-related, equally domesticable roof rat be evaluated on the same six-factor framework (human health, nutrition, habitat, thermoregulation, social behaviour/reproduction, and domestication). Since one of those six factors is domestication itself, it is worth making the point plainly: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised everywhere as domestic animals because what counts is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not wild ancestry — and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, which the assessment criterion is designed to capture. First, contact RVO's helpdesk to confirm the exact steps and what scientific documentation is needed; then, if you are prepared to pursue it, file the formal assessment request.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the LAW AS WRITTEN, specifically the species' ABSENCE from a statutory positive list. The Netherlands uses a "verboden tenzij" (forbidden-unless) positive-list scheme under the Wet dieren / Besluit houders van dieren: only the ~30 mammal species placed on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept, bred or traded. Rattus rattus is simply not on that list. RVO and the NVWA are applying the rule correctly when they say the roof rat may not be kept — so a complaint, an appeal, or a request that the agency "reinterpret" the rule will NOT work, because there is nothing being misread. The lever is to CHANGE WHAT IS ON THE LIST. Crucially, the Dutch system does not require a legislative bill or a one-off public-comment window for this: the regulation contains its own standing rulemaking/petition mechanism. Any belanghebbende (interested party) may file an official "beoordeling aanvragen" with RVO (via Mijn RVO, €500 per species, decision within 6 — extendable to 9 — months), supported by scientific sources on the assessment criteria, and the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst evaluates the species for addition. That is the correct and only effective lever here, and it is administrative rulemaking, not agency reinterpretation. The strong tailwind for the Netherlands: the fancy brown rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica) is ALREADY on the list, which proves a domesticated Rattus line can satisfy the criteria — making the roof-rat case an evidence-driven extension rather than a novel claim.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) — general contact form / helpdesk for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (executive / agency) — official contact page
    RVO administers the positive list and runs the assessment process. Use the helpdesk first to confirm exactly what an assessment request must contain and how an individual files it (DigiD via Mijn RVO). This is the right first touchpoint to understand the official pathway before committing the €500 application fee. Dutch-language form; RVO aims to reply within 3 working days. Phone: 088 042 47 47 (weekdays 08:30-17:00).
  • RVO — official species-assessment request portal ("diersoort laten beoordelen" / Mijn RVO) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the statutory rulemaking lever: the official page describing how an interested party formally requests that a mammal species (here, Rattus rattus) be assessed for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. The actual request is submitted through Mijn RVO (https://mijn.rvo.nl/huisdierenlijst, DigiD login for individuals), costs €500 per species, and gets a decision within 6 months (extendable to 9). This — not an appeal to the agency — is what can actually change the list.
  • NVWA (Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit) — enforcement authority, for status confirmation (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The NVWA enforces which animals may be kept and is the right place to confirm in writing the current keeping status of Rattus rattus before you act. Useful as documentation, but note: the NVWA cannot add a species to the list — that is RVO's assessment process. Dutch-language web form.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to assess the domesticated black rat (Rattus rattus) for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst

To the RVO team responsible for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

I am writing about a domesticated companion animal that is currently kept successfully elsewhere but cannot be kept in the Netherlands: the tame black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus). I understand that since 1 July 2024 only mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst may be kept, and that Rattus rattus is not on it.

I would like to request that a domesticated, captive-bred line of Rattus rattus be assessed for addition to the list. These animals are bred in captivity, are tame and handleable, are kept indoors as pets, and are never released into the wild — exactly like the fancy brown rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica), which is already on the list. The relevant question is therefore the suitability of the kept, domesticated strain against your six assessment criteria, not the behaviour of wild populations. Because domestication is itself one of those six criteria, I would note that wild ancestry alone should not be decisive: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised everywhere as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness rather than its species label. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

Could you please confirm the exact steps for submitting an assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for this species, and what scientific documentation the Adviescollege expects? I am prepared to pursue the formal application.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Nederlands
Onderwerp: Verzoek tot beoordeling van de gedomesticeerde zwarte rat (Rattus rattus) voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst

Geacht RVO-team verantwoordelijk voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

Ik schrijf u over een gedomesticeerd gezelschapsdier dat elders met succes wordt gehouden, maar in Nederland niet gehouden mag worden: de tamme zwarte rat / dakrat (Rattus rattus). Ik begrijp dat sinds 1 juli 2024 alleen zoogdiersoorten op de huis- en hobbydierenlijst gehouden mogen worden, en dat Rattus rattus daar niet op staat.

Graag verzoek ik om een gedomesticeerde, in gevangenschap gefokte lijn van Rattus rattus te laten beoordelen voor opname op de lijst. Deze dieren worden in gevangenschap gefokt, zijn tam en hanteerbaar, worden binnenshuis als huisdier gehouden en worden nooit in het wild losgelaten — precies zoals de tamme bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica), die al op de lijst staat. De relevante vraag is dus de geschiktheid van de gehouden, gedomesticeerde lijn aan de hand van uw zes beoordelingscriteria, en niet het gedrag van wilde populaties. Omdat domesticatie zelf een van die zes criteria is, wijs ik erop dat alleen de wilde afstamming niet doorslaggevend zou mogen zijn: de hond stamt af van de wolf en de kat van een wilde katachtige, en toch worden beide overal erkend als huisdieren, omdat een huisdier wordt bepaald door generaties van fokken in gevangenschap op tamheid en niet door de soortnaam. Een in gevangenschap gefokte zwarte rat is in diezelfde zin gedomesticeerd.

Kunt u mij bevestigen wat de exacte stappen zijn om een beoordeling aan te vragen voor deze soort, en welke wetenschappelijke onderbouwing het Adviescollege verwacht? Ik ben bereid de formele aanvraag in te dienen.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › New Zealand

Summary. New Zealand bars the ship rat (Rattus rattus) at the border and treats it as a top conservation pest, but the keeping picture is more nuanced than a flat ban. The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand, and that there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply). R. rattus is nonetheless central to the Predator Free 2050 programme and is managed as a pest under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and regional pest-management plans; whether private possession of a ship rat specifically (as opposed to the usual pet, the fancy rat R. norvegicus) is restricted under the Biosecurity Act / an unwanted-organism declaration is the open question MPI's welfare team did not resolve. Importing one is firmly prohibited; never release any rat.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.

MPI also confirmed that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand (per MPI's 'Bringing pets to NZ other than cats and dogs' guidance). Note: this welfare-team reply did not address whether the ship rat (Rattus rattus) specifically is restricted for private possession or breeding as a pest / 'unwanted organism' under the Biosecurity Act 1993 or regional pest-management plans.

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there is no Animal Welfare Act 1999 registration or permit to keep rats, so keeping is not permit-gated at the welfare layer. However, R. rattus is a declared conservation pest central to Predator Free 2050 and is managed under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and regional pest-management plans; whether private possession of a ship rat specifically is restricted (for example as an 'unwanted organism') was not addressed by MPI's welfare team. Genuinely unsettled for R. rattus pending a Biosecurity-Act clarification (the fancy rat, R. norvegicus, is the species ordinarily kept as a pet).

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), NZ Department of Conservation, Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there are no Animal Welfare Act registration or permit requirements for breeding rats. As with keeping, the unresolved layer is the Biosecurity Act 1993 / pest-management status of breeding R. rattus specifically — propagating a declared pest may be restricted even though the welfare framework imposes no permit. Unsettled for R. rattus pending Biosecurity confirmation.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), NZ Department of Conservation

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there are no Animal Welfare Act registration or permit requirements for selling rats. The open question is again the Biosecurity Act 1993: 'spreading' or trading a declared pest / unwanted organism can be restricted regardless of the welfare framework. Unsettled for R. rattus specifically pending Biosecurity confirmation.

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand — its 'Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs)' guidance lists rats among animals that may not be imported. Importation is therefore prohibited under NZ's strict biosecurity controls. Internal transport of any lawfully held animal is otherwise subject to the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) code of welfare. Never release.

Sources: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Restrictions & responsibilities

Pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand (MPI, June 2026) — there is no import pathway for a roof rat from any country. Internal transport of a lawfully held animal must meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare. Never release any rat into the environment; R. rattus is a primary Predator Free 2050 eradication target.
  • Do not attempt to import a roof rat into New Zealand — it is not permitted
  • For any internal transport, meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare

Source: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)

Keepers of any animal owe the Animal Welfare Act 1999 duties (meet the animal's physical, health, and behavioural needs; provide treatment for sickness or injury); breaching a minimum standard in a code of welfare can support a prosecution. There is no code of welfare specific to pet rats, but the general duties apply. Never release a rat — release/spread of a pest is a serious biosecurity matter.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Sweden

Summary. Sweden is permissive for the roof rat — now confirmed in writing by the Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket, June 2026). There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and not on Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). The Animal Welfare Act (Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192) regulates HOW animals are kept, not WHICH rodent species, and the Board of Agriculture's rules (SJVFS 2019:15) cover rats generically as gnagare. Jordbruksverket confirmed it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with NO permit and NO registration; only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping/breeding/selling needs to check with the county board (länsstyrelsen) — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT from the permit requirement (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals). Welfare and enclosure standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). Ironically R. rattus is classed as EXTINCT (RE) in the wild in Sweden, so captive pets pose essentially zero invasion risk. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration (commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter); intra-EU commercial movement, or more than 5 pet animals, needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. Non-EU import is tighter.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket), written reply June 2026: it is permitted to keep Rattus rattus as pets in Sweden as long as the animals are not caught in the wild, with NO permit and NO registration required (SJVFS 2019:15, ch. 1 §§4-5). Welfare and enclosure-size/enrichment standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). A permit is only relevant for PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is exempt (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals); professional operators should ask their county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is needed. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration; commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter, and intra-EU commercial movement (or more than 5 pet animals) needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. The agency also confirmed the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with no permit and no registration (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1 §§4-5). Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192 imposes welfare duties but no species ban; R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list and Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). Keepers must meet welfare/enclosure standards (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/furnishing/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18) and the social-species rule (keep ≥2 rats).

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that keeping, breeding, or selling pets other than dogs and cats at larger scale but NOT in a professional manner is EXEMPT from the permit requirement — so a private/hobby rattery needs no permit regardless of cage count. Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) breeding must ask the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is required, and the exemption does NOT cover breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals. (The agency clarified the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.) Welfare standards apply throughout.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Free transfers and sales between hobbyists are permit-free: Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that larger-scale but non-professional keeping/breeding/selling of pets other than dogs and cats is exempt from the permit requirement (Sweden has no separate pet-shop licence). Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) selling must check with the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen). SJVFS 2019:15 sets sale conditions (health checks, documentation). No species ban or price cap on captive-bred R. rattus; the exemption excludes breeding animals sold as feeder/feed animals.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026): cross-border transport of pet rodents needs NO registration. If animals are moved in connection with an economic activity, the carrier must be authorised as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7; minimum rodent-container requirements in Annex/Bilaga 1.11). For intra-EU COMMERCIAL movement, or movement of more than 5 pet animals, no health certificate and no TRACES notification are required, but an Article 151 Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) self-declaration is — issued by the operator at the place of origin, which must itself be registered as an establishment for terrestrial animals (Art. 84). There is no numeric cap on a single commercial movement and no fixed template for the self-declaration. Non-EU import follows different, tighter rules. Internal transport is unregulated beyond welfare. Never release.

Sources: Jordbruksverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling of pet rodents needs to check with your county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) about a permit — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT (Jordbruksverket, June 2026), except breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals, which is not exempt. Transport in connection with an economic activity requires authorisation as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7). Meet the welfare rules (minimum enclosure size, enrichment, and keep rats in groups of ≥2). Never release a roof rat.
  • If operating professionally, ask your länsstyrelsen whether a permit is required
  • For transport in connection with an economic activity, register as an authorised animal transporter with Jordbruksverket

Where: Länsstyrelsen (county administrative board); Jordbruksverket for transporter authorisation

Source: Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Singapore? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Singapore

Summary. Singapore prohibits the roof rat as a pet, completely. It runs a closed 'positive list': only species the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS, a cluster under the National Parks Board) has approved may be kept. The approved small-mammal list includes the domestic mouse (Mus musculus) alongside rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas — but NO species of the genus Rattus, so neither the roof rat (R. rattus) nor the ordinary fancy rat (R. norvegicus) may be kept. Because it is not a listed pet, R. rattus defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965, and s.5C(1) makes it a strict-liability offence to keep any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval (no such approval is available to the public). Breeding is separately barred by the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA), which defines any rodent 'capable of carrying' disease as a public-health vector and, under s.16, prohibits breeding vectors without permission; sale/transfer is blocked by the Wildlife Act (s.8) and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules (the hobbyist breeding exemption applies only to approved 'relevant pet animals'). The ONLY lawful pathway for any Rattus is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) may import and keep lab rats — never a private pet keeper. One statutory quirk: the Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 cull-list names R. norvegicus and R. tanezumi (and Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus) as exempt from the s.5C culling ban, but R. rattus is omitted, so a strict reading paradoxically gives the wild roof rat unpermitted-culling protection denied its cousins — an anomaly that offers a pet keeper nothing. Not CITES-listed; the closed positive list, not CITES, is the operative bar.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

R. rattus is not on the AVS approved-pet positive list (which permits mice, rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas — no Rattus), so it defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965. Section 5C(1) provides that 'a person must not intentionally kill, trap, take or keep any wildlife in any place unless the person has the Director-General's written approval to do so' — a strict-liability offence (belief that the animal is a domesticated pet is no defence), carrying up to S$20,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment for a first offence. The Wildlife Act's domestic-animal carve-outs (dogs, cats, livestock, poultry) do not include any rat, and no public permit/registration pathway exists to keep a roof rat. AVS guidance also treats rats as vermin that will not be allowed.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding is interdicted by public-health law independent of the keeping ban. The Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA) s.2 defines a 'vector' to include 'any rodent, including its young, which is carrying or causing, or capable of carrying or causing, any disease to human beings' — the test is the species' biological capacity, so a captive-bred, pathogen-free R. rattus is still a vector. CVPA s.16 ('Prohibition on breeding, etc., of vectors without Director-General's permission') makes it a strict criminal offence to intentionally breed vectors; no private hobbyist permit is ever issued (penalties under s.23 run to large fines and imprisonment). The only entities permitted to breed Rattus are licensed Animal Research Facilities. Keeping the animal to breed it is independently barred under the Wildlife Act s.5C, so a hobbyist breeding programme is doubly unlawful.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Sale or transfer (including giving away free) is blocked on two layers. (1) Wildlife Act 1965 s.8 prohibits selling, offering for sale, or exporting any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval; doing so in the course of an animal-related business is aggravated (s.5C(3)(b)(i): up to S$20,000 / 12 months even on a first offence). (2) The Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules require an AVS pet-shop/breeding licence to distribute, breed, exhibit or sell pet animals (Rule 4), and AVS will not licence the sale of a non-positive-listed species. The Schedule 1 hobbyist 'breed-and-give-away-for-adoption' exemption applies only to a 'relevant pet animal or bird' — which excludes all Rattus — so it is legally void for the roof rat. Therefore one cannot lawfully sell, trade, or give away a roof rat in Singapore.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Import/export of animals requires an AVS import licence under the Animals and Birds Act 1965 s.7 (no person may import any animal without the Director-General's licence). The framework bifurcates rodents into two mutually exclusive paths. PERSONAL PET import is allowed only for positive-listed small mammals — the AVS pet-import page lists rabbits, mice, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs and chinchillas, and the GoBusiness licensing system summarily rejects a personal pet application for any Rattus species; so personal import/transport of a roof rat is effectively PROHIBITED. The ONLY lawful pathway is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules may import lab 'rats' from an AVS-approved overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate, pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine (import licence ~S$174 express). That route is closed to private citizens. Not CITES-listed. Never release.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat cannot lawfully be kept, bred, sold, given away, or imported as a pet in Singapore. No Rattus species is on the AVS approved-pet positive list (only the mouse, Mus musculus, among small rodents), so the roof rat is 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965 — keeping it without the Director-General's written approval is a strict-liability offence under s.5C (up to S$20,000 / 12 months), breeding it is barred as a public-health 'vector' under CVPA 1998 s.16, and selling/transferring it is barred under Wildlife Act s.8 and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules. The ban is genus-wide (the ordinary fancy rat R. norvegicus is barred too). There is no private permit, licence, or hobbyist exemption. Never release.
  • Do not keep, breed, sell, give away, or import a roof rat in Singapore — no private permit pathway exists (Wildlife Act s.5C; CVPA s.16; Animals and Birds Act / pet-shop rules)
  • Never release a roof rat (it is a documented public-health vector and pest)

Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), National Parks Board

Source: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

The only lawful route by which any Rattus may be imported, bred or kept in Singapore is institutional research. An accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules — with an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), an attending veterinarian and AVS oversight — may import lab rats from an AVS-approved overseas facility under a commercial veterinary health certificate, with pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine. This pathway is closed to private individuals and confers no private pet-keeping right.
  • (Institutions only) Hold a valid AVS Animal Research Facility (ARF) licence with an IACUC and attending veterinarian
  • Import lab rats only from an AVS-accredited overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate
  • Book border-control inspection at least 5 days before arrival; complete inspection and quarantine on arrival

Forms: AVS — Importing and exporting laboratory animals, GoBusiness — Licence for Animal Research Facility · Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks (ARF licence + import licence via GoBusiness) · Fees: Import licence for non-food animals/biologics ~S$174 (express, issued one working day after submission)

Source: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Singapore. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Act 1965 (2020 Revised Edition) — s.5C (no keeping/killing/trapping/taking wildlife without Director-General approval), s.8 (sale/export of wildlife), s.2 'wildlife' definition, s.6 'defence of property' — Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks
  • Animals and Birds Act 1965 — prevention of epizootic disease; s.7 import licence; premises licensing power — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)
  • Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 — s.2 'vector' (rodent capable of carrying disease), s.16 (prohibition on breeding vectors without Director-General permission), s.23 (penalties) — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA
  • Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 — Schedule exempts R. norvegicus, R. tanezumi, Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus from the s.5C culling ban; R. rattus omitted — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; made under Wildlife Act 1965

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States

Summary. Under U.S. federal law, KEEPING a roof rat as a pet is unregulated (left to the states). But the common belief that all rats are federally exempt is wrong for Rattus rattus: the Animal Welfare Act's rat exclusion covers only research-bred rats, so commercial BREEDERS and SELLERS can need a USDA license (small hobby breeders and face-to-face sales/giveaways are exempt), and because the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife,' IMPORTING or EXPORTING one requires a Form 3-177 wildlife declaration even for a captive-bred pet.

legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate private, non-commercial possession of pet rats; under the Tenth Amendment this is left to state, county, and municipal law. Rattus rattus is not federally listed as injurious or endangered, so nothing federal stops you from keeping one (your state/city may).

Sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Pet roof rats are NOT exempt from the Animal Welfare Act (its exclusion covers only rats 'bred for use in research,' 7 U.S.C. 2132(g); 9 C.F.R. 1.1), so they are regulated 'animals.' But a USDA license is needed ONLY if you sell the offspring WHOLESALE (to resellers) or SIGHT-UNSEEN (shipped to a buyer who has not seen the animal). Selling or placing rats face-to-face to the final owner, or giving them away, is exempt as a 'retail' transaction with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 2.1(a)(3)). The 'four or fewer breeding females' exemption only matters for sight-unseen/shipped sales.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

A USDA Class B dealer license is required only for WHOLESALE sales (to resellers/pet stores) or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipped sales. Selling face-to-face to the final owner (a 'retail pet store' transaction, which includes a home breeder selling directly), and giving rats away, are exempt — with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 1.1, 2.1(a)(3)). Only a wholesale or sight-unseen seller keeping 5 or more breeding females must be licensed.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a roof rat between U.S. states needs no federal permit (and since U.S. v. Zinke (2017) even injurious species may move between contiguous states), BUT the Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. 3372) makes it a federal crime to transport one into a state where it is illegal. IMPORT/EXPORT is more involved: the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife' (only Rattus norvegicus is on the domesticated-exemption list, 50 C.F.R. 14.4), so each shipment needs a USFWS Form 3-177 declaration, entry/exit through a designated wildlife port, and an inspection fee, even for a captive-bred pet (the personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial license). The CDC African-rodent import ban (42 C.F.R. 71.56) does not apply to roof rats sourced outside Africa, and USDA Veterinary Services has no health requirements for pet-rodent import.

Sources: U.S. Code, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS, CDC, USFWS

A USDA APHIS license (Class A breeder / Class B dealer) is required ONLY for WHOLESALE selling or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipping by someone keeping 5 or more breeding females. Selling face-to-face to the final owner, or giving rats away, is EXEMPT no matter how many breeding females you keep (the 'retail pet store' exemption, 9 CFR 2.1(a)(3)).
  • Check whether you exceed the exemption thresholds (9 CFR 2.1(a)(3))
  • If not exempt, apply for the appropriate USDA license and meet the 9 CFR Part 3 housing/care standards

Forms: USDA AWA licensing rule & exemptions (9 CFR 2.1) · Where: USDA APHIS Animal Care · Fees: Varies by license type/size

Source: USDA-APHIS, USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code

Importing or exporting a roof rat requires a USFWS wildlife declaration (Form 3-177), clearance at a designated wildlife port, and a per-shipment inspection fee, because Rattus rattus is legally 'wildlife' (it is not on the 50 CFR 14.4 domesticated list). The personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial Import/Export license, not the declaration, port, or inspection.

Rattus rattus is listed Category 1b under the 2020 NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Regulations, a designation tied to offshore islands. So keeping is open while breeding, trade and movement are effectively closed to hobbyists (a containment regime). A separate provincial layer can add a 'wild animal in captivity' permit in some provinces (liaise with your provincial environmental department), and international import is handled separately by the National Department of Agriculture's State Veterinary import permit. ⚠️ Live advocacy window: DFFE confirmed the AIS list amendment is under Law Reform review and will be gazetted for PUBLIC COMMENT this financial year — the moment to engage on how the species is treated.

Summary. Alberta is the strictest jurisdiction in Canada — and one of the strictest anywhere. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the ENTIRE genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the law prohibits the import, purchase, sale, transport, and possession of any live rat. There is NO exemption for 'fancy', tame, or captive-bred rats. The only legal route is a special Ministerial permit reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, or approved labs. A pet roof rat in Alberta may be seized and destroyed, and the keeper fined. Alberta has defended its 'rat-free' status since 1950.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alberta-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alberta is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Agricultural Pests Act declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and possession of a live rat by a private citizen is unlawful — Alberta enforces a zero-tolerance 'rat-free' policy. There is explicitly no exemption for fancy, tame, or domesticated rats; a single caged pet is treated as an unacceptable escape risk. Wild sightings are reported to the 310-RATS line and eradicated.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding requires possession, which is prohibited, and the statute separately forbids the purchase, sale, or distribution of a declared pest. There is no legal hobby or commercial breeding of rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling, giving, or otherwise distributing a live rat is expressly prohibited as dealing in a declared pest. No pet-trade layer exists for rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transporting a live rat into or within Alberta is prohibited except under a highly restricted Ministerial permit (research institutions, zoos, approved labs only). Whether a non-resident may drive a securely caged pet rat continuously THROUGH Alberta without stopping is not clearly addressed in the published rules — we have asked the province to clarify. Treat any presence of a rat in Alberta as prohibited unless you hold a permit.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Restrictions & responsibilities

The only lawful way to possess, breed, or transport a rat in Alberta is a special permit issued by the Minister of Agriculture, available only to accredited research institutions, major zoos, or government-approved laboratories — not to private pet keepers.
  • Pet keeping is not permitted — there is no pet-owner permit

Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation (Ministerial permit)

Source: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

If you move to Alberta, you cannot bring a pet rat with you. Rehome it responsibly before relocating; do not transport it into the province. Rat sightings are reported to 310-RATS (310-7287) and acted on.

Source: Government of Alberta

Alberta's only legal route to hold any Rattus is a Ministerial Form-6 permit (AR 184/2001 s.11) limited to research facilities, zoos, and inspectors — no private/hobby pathway. Even the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is prohibited for private keeping.

Forms: AR 184/2001 Form 6 — Ministerial permit to keep rats (research/zoo/inspector only) · Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Inspection and Investigation Section

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alberta. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alberta

Alberta is one of the only places on Earth with a true, total ban on keeping any pet rat. Under the Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the ENTIRE genus Rattus — every rat species, including the ordinary tame "fancy" pet rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) — is a declared agricultural pest. The Government of Alberta states plainly: "It is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." Possession, import, purchase, sale, transport, and breeding of any live rat are all prohibited. The only permit (a Ministerial permit under AR 184/2001) is reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, and government labs — there is no private or hobby pathway, not even for a single captive-bred, tame rat kept indoors in a cage. Penalties can reach $5,000 per animal, and a pet rat found in the province can be seized and destroyed. This ban is the backbone of Alberta's 75-year "rat-free" status, and it makes no distinction between a wild invasive rat and a domesticated companion animal that has never lived outdoors.

The ask: Ask the Legislative Assembly (your MLA) to amend the Agricultural Pests Act / Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation to create a narrow, well-defined exemption for domesticated, captive-bred pet rats kept indoors under reasonable conditions (for example: spayed/neutered or single-sex housing, secure escape-proof caging, microchipping or registration, and a ban on outdoor release) — distinct from Alberta's wild-rat eradication program, which would continue unchanged. Be clear and honest about what this is NOT: do not ask the rat-control program or Alberta Agriculture to "make an exception," because that office is correctly applying a law it cannot rewrite. The change has to come from the Legislature.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the problem is the LAW AS WRITTEN, not a bureaucracy misreading it. The Agricultural Pests Act and AR 184/2001 declare the whole genus Rattus a pest at the statutory/regulatory level, and the rat-control agency is correctly and deliberately applying that prohibition — the Government of Alberta's own website confirms "It is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." There is no exemption list a tame or captive-bred rat could be added to, and the sole permit category is statutorily confined to research/zoo/lab operators. Therefore appealing to the agency (rats@gov.ab.ca / 310-FARM) will NOT change anything — that line exists to report and eradicate rats, and the staff there have no authority to legalize pet keeping. The only lever that can change this is the Legislature: amending the Act or the Regulation to carve out a domesticated-pet-rat exemption. Practically, that means writing to your MLA (and, where relevant, the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation in their legislative/policy capacity). The single narrow thing the agency CAN properly answer is a factual clarification (e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet rat through the province) — included only as a secondary, agency-appropriate touchpoint, not as the reform lever.

  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Members of the Legislative Assembly directory (Find Your MLA / Member Contact list) (legislature) — official contact page
    The total ban is set in statute (Agricultural Pests Act) and regulation (AR 184/2001). Only the Legislature can amend it, so your own MLA is the correct first touchpoint. This official directory lists all 87 MLAs by name and constituency with individual contact pages and a downloadable contact list, letting you reach the representative who can raise or sponsor a change.
  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Find Your MLA by riding (Elections Alberta MLA search) (legislature) — official contact page
    Use this official Elections Alberta tool to identify exactly which MLA represents your address/riding before you write, so your letter reaches your own representative (constituent letters carry the most weight).

    Included only for a narrow factual question this office can legitimately answer — e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet Rattus through Alberta. That balance is yours to strike, and Alberta's wild-rat eradication program would continue unchanged.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › California

Summary. California restricts ALL rodents as 'detrimental' wild animals (14 CCR §671), and CDFW never issues possession permits for pets — so a normal wild-type roof rat is effectively illegal to keep. BUT the rule exempts 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)', and that exemption is written by phenotype/origin, not by species — it doesn't name Rattus norvegicus. So a white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared Rattus rattus may qualify, while a wild-type one does not. Whether a domesticated roof-rat line qualifies is the open question we've put to CDFW.

legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the California-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where California is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

California classifies every species of Order Rodentia as a 'detrimental' restricted wild animal (14 CCR §671; FGC §2118), and CDFW categorically refuses Restricted Species Permits for PET purposes (only research/exhibition/education). The one opening is the exemption for 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)' (14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c)) — which is defined by phenotype/origin, NOT by species. A white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat may qualify; a phenotypically wild-type (agouti/black) roof rat is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Wild-caught roof rats can never be kept (FGC §3005.5).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding restricted rodents is prohibited without research/exhibition permits. If the animals meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, breeding is outside CDFW's wildlife jurisdiction — but local animal-control/zoning rules apply, and any retail sale is governed by the Pet Store Animal Care Act.

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling restricted wild rodents is prohibited. Selling EXEMPT domesticated rats is legal but regulated by California's Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361), which sets enclosure, space, enrichment, and veterinary-care standards for anyone selling vertebrate pets.

Sources: CA Health & Safety Code, CA Code of Regulations

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Importing/transporting a restricted rodent needs a permit + Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. An EXEMPT domesticated rat may cross state lines without a restricted-species permit, but every animal entering California is still subject to inspection at CDFA border stations (the roof rat is a top agricultural pest), so carry documentation that the animal is an exempt domestic race. International movement is restricted federally (USFWS Form 3-177 — see United States).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

If the roof rat does NOT meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, it is a restricted species and CDFW issues permits only for research/exhibition/education — NOT pets — so keeping/breeding it as a pet is effectively prohibited (and wild-caught roof rats can never be kept, FGC §3005.5). Restricted-facility permits carry steep application + inspection fees and an emergency action plan.
  • Determine whether your animal meets the white/albino/trained/laboratory-reared exemption
  • If exempt, no CDFW permit is needed; if not, pet possession is not permitted

Forms: CDFW Restricted Species Permits · Where: CDFW License & Revenue Branch, Special Permits Unit · Fees: Restricted-species permits are not issued for pets

Source: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Retail sale of an exempt domestic rat must meet the Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361): structurally sound enclosures, adequate space, enrichment, separation of sick animals, and veterinary care.

Source: CA Health & Safety Code

Where: CDFA border protection stations

Source: CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Source: CA Code of Regulations
